steps.html:
Left-brained or right-brained: one of the most repeated ideas about the mind, and one that the research never supported. Two texts about where it came from, and about the duller thing that turns out to be true.

steps.title: The words that tell you where the argument is going
steps.html:
Read this before the texts. You will use it immediately.

A linker is a signpost. It tells you, before you read the sentence, what that sentence is going to do to the one before it.

Adding: moreover, in addition, furthermore, what is more. Contrasting: however, nevertheless, on the other hand, although, whereas. Result: therefore, so, as a result, consequently. Restating: in other words, that is to say. Example: for example, for instance, such as.

The most useful ones for reading are the contrast linkers, because they mark the turn in an argument. When you see However, Nevertheless, or Although, the writer is about to take something back or push against what they just said.

Nevertheless is worth knowing precisely: it means despite that, this is still true. It concedes and then refuses to give way.

Practical technique: when you skim a text, read the linkers and the sentence that follows each one. That is usually where the argument lives.

steps.title: Which linker tells you the writer is about to disagree with what they just said?
steps.why: Moreover adds, for instance illustrates. Only nevertheless concedes and then pushes back.

steps.title: How the left-brain myth got started
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 148 words

In the 1960s, researchers carried out experiments on patients whose brain hemispheres had been surgically separated. They found out that the two sides handled different tasks. So far, so accurate.

What happened next was not their fault. Popular writers picked the findings up and made up a much larger claim: that people are either logical left-brained types or creative right-brained ones. Personality tests began to pop up everywhere, and self-help books promised to convert you.

However, the research never said any such thing. Although the two hemispheres do specialise, no study has ever turned up evidence that individuals are dominated by one side. Nevertheless, the idea refuses to die out.

The reason is not that people are stupid. It is that the myth sorts out something awkward — why some things come easily and others do not — and offers an answer that takes no work.

steps.title: What the myth is covering up
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 149 words

Nevertheless, the question underneath it is a real one. Why do some people come up with ideas easily while others, who are just as able, run out of them within minutes?

The research that has been carried out on this suggests something less flattering than a brain type. It turns out that the strongest predictor is how many ideas a person is willing to produce before stopping. Those who set up a target of twenty ideas reach better ones than those who aim for three, even though most of the twenty are useless.

In other words, the difference is not the quality of the first idea but the willingness to keep going after it. Therefore the practical advice is dull: do not try to work out the best answer immediately. Instead, phase out the habit of stopping early.

Whether that is what anybody wants to hear is another matter.

steps.title: The patterns in one place
steps.html:
Lessons 33 and 34 together, plus what happens after a phrasal verb.

After a verb: some take -ing (admit, deny, avoid, finish, keep, suggest), some take the infinitive (decide, refuse, manage, hope, intend, agree), and six change meaning (remember, forget, stop, try, regret, go on).

After a preposition: always -ing. This includes the particle in many phrasal verbs: come up with solving it, fed up with waiting, the habit of stopping.

As a subject: -ing. Stopping early is the problem.

For purpose: the infinitive. They set up a website to test it.

The trap in this lesson: a phrasal verb ending in a preposition takes -ing, but one ending in an adverb particle can be followed by an infinitive. Compare They came up with testing it (with is a preposition) and They set out to test it (out is a particle, and the infinitive gives the purpose).

Promise + infinitive.

do not try to work out the best answer immediately
Try to = attempt.

phase out the habit of stopping early

steps.title: Which form after a phrasal verb
steps.html:
1. Two phrasal verbs, two different answers.
  2. come up with ends in with, which is a preposition. Anything after it is a noun or an -ing form: They came up with testing it on students.
  3. set out ends in out, which is an adverb particle, not a preposition. It can be followed by an infinitive of purpose: They set out to test it on students.
  4. The test: can the particle take an object directly? with must (with something), so it is a preposition. out need not be, so it is a particle.
  5. In practice, learn the whole phrase. Look forward to, get round to, come up with, be used to all end in prepositions and all take -ing.

steps.title: You are going to write an argument.

options.label: A widely believed idea about learning that is wrong
Why a dull piece of advice works better than an exciting one
Something you were told about yourself that turned out not to be true
How you actually come up with ideas

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least four linkers, including one contrast linker, and at least four phrasal verbs with out or up.
steps.placeholder: I was told for years that …
steps.html:
• Open with the belief and where you met it.
  • Turn on it with <i>However</i> or <i>Nevertheless</i>.
  • Concede something real with <i>Although</i>.
  • Restate with <i>In other words</i>.
  • Close with a result, using <i>Therefore</i>.

Useful language

  • Research carried out in … found out that …
  • However / Nevertheless, …
  • Although … , no study has ever turned up evidence that …
  • It turns out that …
  • In other words, …
  • Therefore the practical advice is …
steps.modelHtml:
The ten-minute rule

I was told for years that I was not a morning person, and I made decisions on that basis for most of my twenties. However, when I finally worked out where the belief came from, it turned out to be one comment made by a teacher in 1998.

The research that has been carried out on this is not flattering to anybody. Although people do differ genuinely in their body clocks, most of what we call a 'type' is a habit we have set up and then stopped questioning.

In other words, the label saves us the work of finding out what is actually true. Nevertheless, it survives, because it explains a real difficulty and costs nothing.

Therefore the dull advice: try the thing you have decided you cannot do, for ten minutes, before you rule it out.
